keyECGEvidence: Ventricular Rate 96 bpm, Atrial Rate 96 bpm, Regular
ST deviation: Diffuse concave (upward-scooping) ST elevation 1-2 mm in leads I, II, aVL, aVF, V3-V6; PR-segment depression in leads II, III, aVF, V4-V6; PR elevation in aVR
Pre-event note: chest pain sharp, pleuritic, worse supine, improved leaning forward
modelResponse.mechanism: Inflammatory process causing pericardial irritation and myocardial involvement, manifesting as diffuse ST elevation and PR changes.
contributingFactors: Elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 4.8 mg/dL, ESR 38 mm/hr)

rejectedAlternatives.why: The ECG findings are diffuse concave ST elevation with reciprocal changes (PR depression) rather than localized STEMI patterns, and the clinical context strongly suggests pericardial involvement (pleuritic pain, friction rub).
While tachycardia is present, the specific ECG pattern of diffuse ST elevation and PR changes is more characteristic of pericarditis than primary thyroid cardiac effects.

The clinical presentation (pleuritic pain relieved by leaning forward) and ECG findings (diffuse ST changes) are less typical for ischemic ACS, despite the elevated troponin T 0.03 ng/mL (which is likely secondary to inflammation/myocarditis).

recommendedActions: Administer NSAIDs (e.g., Ibuprofen) or Aspirin as per protocol for pericarditis management, while monitoring renal function.
Initiate cardiac monitoring and serial ECGs to track resolution of ST changes.
Obtain serial inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) and echocardiogram to assess pericardial effusion/rictus.
Maintain hemodynamic monitoring and ensure airway management readiness (Full code status).
uncertainty: The definitive diagnosis between pericarditis and myocarditis cannot be made without imaging (Echo) or biopsy, but the clinical picture is highly suggestive of an inflammatory cardiac process.
